data_points.claim: Rayleigh scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength (1/lambda^4); blue light (~450nm) is scattered roughly 6-10x more than red light (~700nm) — (700/400)^4 ~= 9.4
Air molecules act like tiny antennas: incoming light makes their charges oscillate, and the re-radiated power scales with frequency^4 — which is where the fourth-power law comes from

Violet light actually scatters MORE than blue, but the sky isn't violet because the sun emits less violet, the upper atmosphere absorbs some of it, and human eyes are far less sensitive to violet than blue
data_points.source_name: University of Arizona atmospheric sciences lecture notes

data_points.claim: The explanation was built over 52 years: Tyndall's 1859 experiments, Rayleigh's 1871 fourth-power formula, and Einstein's 1911 calculation settling that air molecules themselves (not dust) do the scattering
Sunsets are red for the same reason the sky is blue: at low sun angles light passes through so much more air that even green and yellow get scattered away, leaving red to reach your eyes directly
The sky-reflects-the-ocean myth is easily refuted: the sky is just as blue in deserts and inland areas far from any sea

misconceptions.myth: The sky is blue because it reflects the blue of the oceans
misconceptions.reality: The sky is blue everywhere — deserts included. Air molecules scatter short (blue) wavelengths of sunlight far more than long (red) ones

misconceptions.myth: Blue is simply 'the color that scatters most'
misconceptions.reality: Violet scatters even more than blue; the sky looks blue because of the sun's spectrum, atmospheric absorption of violet, and human eye cone sensitivity

research_brief.research_summary: The single most important insight: everyone 'knows' the answer is Rayleigh scattering, but almost nobody knows the two things that make it genuinely interesting — (1) the fourth-power law means blue scatters ~6-10x more than red, which also explains red sunsets and pale horizons in one stroke, and (2) violet scatters even MORE than blue, so the sky's color is ultimately decided inside the human eye. A short animated explainer that leads with the violet paradox, lands the 1/lambda^4 stat visually, and closes on the sunset connection fills a real gap: existing content is either too shallow (one-liners, quiz gimmicks) or too deep (dipole math). The topic remains evergreen and still pulls large short-form audiences (xkcd's April 2026 short: 586K views).
